BlackRock and IFM Investors are in exclusive talks to buy STACK Infrastructure's Asia-Pacific data centres from Blue Owl Capital, in a deal that could be worth up to $25 billion. It is worth a closer look, because it is a different kind of AI infrastructure deal to the ones filling everyone's feed lately.

Most of the recent headlines have been about building new capacity, or lending against contracts for capacity that does not exist yet. This one is the reverse. Stack's Asia-Pacific portfolio is a working business, real data centres in Tokyo, Osaka, Sydney and Melbourne, with tenants already in them and rent already being paid. The buyers are not taking a construction risk. They are buying stabilised, cash-generating assets and the long-term income attached to them.

The make-up of the buying group matters. BlackRock's AI Infrastructure Partnership pools capital from strategic names like Microsoft, NVIDIA and MGX alongside its own funds, and IFM is Australian pension money. That is patient, long-hold institutional capital looking for steady yield, not a quick flip.

On how a deal like this would likely be financed, since the terms are not out yet. Expect a large slug of equity from the consortium, probably somewhere around half the price, with debt raised against the assets covering the rest. Because these are operating data centres with contracted lease income, they support a lot more leverage, and cheaper leverage, than a site still under construction. The usual path is bank acquisition financing to get the deal done quickly, then a refinancing into longer-dated debt, whether that is portfolio-level secured bonds, securitisation of the lease cash flows, or some combination.

The currency side is the part a structurer would enjoy. The assets sit in Japan and Australia and earn yen and Australian dollars. The sensible move is to fund them in those same currencies, borrowing cheaply in yen against the Japanese sites especially, so the debt is matched to the income and there is no currency mismatch to manage. That local funding also pulls in Asian banks and, increasingly, insurance and private credit money looking for exactly this sort of long, stable, asset-backed exposure.

For Blue Owl, selling now turns a platform it built into cash it can recycle into the next thing. That is the infrastructure cycle doing what it is supposed to. Someone builds and assembles the assets, long-term capital buys them once they are proven, and the freed-up money goes back to work.

Deals like this are a healthy sign. They show the AI build-out maturing into something institutional capital can own and finance the way it already owns airports, ports and power grids. That is a far deeper pool of money than the venture and construction funding that got this started, and it is only just beginning to move in.

Prior AI data annotation or model evaluation work
Phonetics or linguistics background
Experience with audio editing or waveform tools

You listen, judge, and submit. Where you find an error, you tag every applicable error code and explain in plain language why the task passed or failed. Critical errors are called out first. You'll complete a short calibration phase before production work begins.

U.S federal guidance confirms AI produces 

records (NARA). Those records must be governed by law. Every organization needs to understand this.

AI produces artifacts (information).Those artifacts become records when they support a business decision.

Prompts, outputs, logs, model versions, these are AI artifacts, not automatic records.They become AI records only when they serve as evidence.

Here is how to govern your AI records:

1. AI records fit inside the records you already manage

Every organization already keeps:

Customer records — complaints, service requests
Employee records — hiring decisions, performance notes
Financial records — approvals, invoices
Operational records — incidents, vendor evaluations

If an AI artifact supports one of these records, it becomes part of that record.

2. AI records follow the same retention laws as your existing records

If you don’t follow the Federal Records Act (FRA). You must follow your industry laws:

Finance: SEC Rule 17a4 → 7 years
Healthcare: HIPAA → 6 years
Employment: EEOC and OSHA → 3 years
Contracts: expiration plus 6 years

➡️ AI logs: can be kept for 2 years

When an AI artifact becomes evidence, it follows the same retention rule as the underlying record.

3. Govern AI records using your existing retention schedule

You don’t need a new AI retention schedule. You extend the one you already have:

1. Add the AI artifact used as evidence
2. Keep it for the same retention period
3. Store it where the record lives
4. Treat AI records exactly like the records they support. Same rules. Same retention. Same destruction.
5. Destroy it the same way you destroy the record

This is how organizations govern AI records right now.

The rule is simple

If an AI artifact is used as evidence, it becomes a record. If it is a record, it follows the same retention and destruction rules.

AI doesn’t change retention. AI doesn’t override the law. AI changes where the evidence comes from.

This is how organizations govern AI records.

URGENT REQUIRED HIRING: Sonic Audit Specialist — German

Rate: $41.5/hour
Type: Hourly Contract, Remote
Schedule: Flexible

About the Role:
We are hiring native and near-native German speakers to audit AI training data in their own language, not to produce it.

You'll work across two Amazon Sonic audit collections:
Multilingual Transcription Audit: Listen to recordings of human or agent speech, read the transcription an annotator produced, and judge whether it accurately captures what the speaker said. Apply a fixed set of error codes, assign a pass or fail verdict, and write a short rationale.
Forced Alignment Audit: Review audio segmented at word level by an automated system. Verify start and end timestamps match the word's actual boundaries and that the reference transcription matches the spoken form. Correct boundaries, split/merge segments, or add/remove segments where the machine got it wrong.
Both collections run at 5.00 audit hours per task.

Who We're Looking For:
Native or near-native command of German as spoken in Germany (born and raised in the region, or fully fluent with 5+ years of residence) – hard requirement
Strong English reading and writing – all conventions, error codes, and rationales are in English
Disciplined rubric application – consistent across hundreds of judgments
Careful listening – distinguish similar sounds, identify word boundaries, tell genuine acoustic ambiguity from annotator error
Prior transcription, subtitling, localization, linguistic annotation, or QA experience is a strong signal

Helpful But Not Required:
Prior AI data annotation or model evaluation work
Phonetics or linguistics background
Experience with audio editing or waveform tools

What the Work Looks Like:
You listen, judge, and submit. Where you find an error, you tag every applicable error code and explain in plain language why the task passed or failed. Critical errors are called out first. You'll complete a short calibration phase before production work begins.

Logistics:
Independent contractor role
Fully remote, flexible schedule
Weekly payments via Stripe or Wise
Unable to support H1-B or STEM OPT candidates

Most remote job advice is written for people already living where the jobs are.

If you're applying from outside that circle, the advice barely applies and nobody tells you.

Here's what actually works when you're competing from a different country and time zone: 👇

1/ Stop applying to job boards first

Public remote listings get thousands of applicants within days. Many are already filled internally before they're posted.

The roles that go to people abroad usually come from smaller companies that were never going to get thousands of applicants in the first place.

2/ Target companies that already hire across borders

A company that has never employed anyone outside its own country has no process for it. Payroll, contracts, tax, none of it exists yet, and you will not be the reason they build it.

A company with people in four countries already has the paperwork solved. Check their team page before you spend an hour on an application.

3/ Solve the time zone question before they ask it

Work out honestly how many hours you overlap with their working day. If it's four or more, say so in your first message and say when.

If it's one or two, apply to async-first companies instead and stop wasting applications on roles that need live collaboration.

4/ Make something they can click

A CV says you can do the work. A link proves it. A small public project, a write-up of how you solved something, a repository, a portfolio page. One is enough. It does more than three extra bullet points ever will.

5/ Write shorter applications than you think you should

Most applications from candidates abroad are too long. Long reads as anxious. Two or three sentences that name the job's real problem and show one piece of evidence beats four paragraphs about your background.

6/ Apply for the job they're actually hiring for

Read past the title. Somewhere in the posting is the problem they want solved. Address that problem in your first line. Most applicants describe themselves instead, which is why most applications look identical.

7/ Expect to be a contractor

Most companies hiring internationally will engage you as a contractor rather than an employee. That usually means no benefits, and tax handled by you.

Know this before you negotiate, not after. For anything with real tax or visa consequences, pay a professional to check it.

8/ Do not let them set a local price

Some companies adjust pay to your country. Some pay the same rate everywhere. The second group exists and is worth finding.

Know the range for the role in their market before you name any number.

9/ Be visible in your first month

The main risk in remote work is not being unproductive. It's being forgotten.
Send a short weekly update whether or not anyone asked for one. Progress, what's blocked, what you need. It takes five minutes and it is the difference between being known and being invisible.

Over the past four years, I’ve worked across IT services and an AI platform, using email, LinkedIn, events, and content to start conversations that turn into business. I’ve also seen a content plan I developed bring in contracts - a good reminder that the next opportunity doesn’t always come from another follow-up.

Now I’m looking for a remote BDR or Lead Generation role where I can take ownership of outbound, build on what works, and have room to test my own ideas.

I bring curiosity, persistence, and a healthy respect for the fact that nobody opens LinkedIn hoping to receive another sales pitch.

If your team is hiring, I’d love an introduction. And if you’re also writing your “open to work” post: apparently, we’re all in sales now. 🙂

Last night, Automo passed 500,000 users.  it took Nine weeks.

I should be celebrating. Instead, I keep thinking about how different this feels from the last time.  When we built Desygner, reaching our first million users took 13 months.

We were competing with Canva. They built an extraordinary company. From where I sat, their access to capital gave them an enormous advantage in hiring, distribution and the ability to keep investing.  We felt that gap every day.

I know what it feels like to have the ambition and the product, but watch a better resourced competitor pull ahead.  This time, I believe the economics are changing.

I can now take on work that once needed an entire team. Decades of experience help me decide what to build, what to reject and when the AI is confidently wrong.

Our hardest hiring problem is finding more people like my cofounders: people with judgement, ownership and a deep commitment to customers.

We have lived this change ourselves.
- 98 people became 12.
- Two month release cycles became twice a day.
- We rebuilt how we develop, test, review and ship software.

Human judgement matters more than ever.

Here is my prediction:
The next 12 months will be brutal for software companies whose costs and processes assume building software must remain slow and expensive.
- Some will adapt brilliantly.
- Some will cut prices and squeeze margins.
- Some, I believe, will disappear.

Having thousands of employees is a dangerous advantage if your business needs thousands of employees just to stand still.

Customers will ask:
Why am I paying for ten subscriptions, paying to connect them, then paying again for AI to work across them?

That is the integration tax. Businesses pay it in money, time and mistakes.

We are building Automo to remove it. One connected platform for running a business, with agents able to work across it.

Ciao.dev is how we build it.  My background is in systems for financial markets. That experience taught me to care about what happens after the demo: permissions, testing, reliability and what happens when something breaks.

Generating software is only part of the job. Being able to trust it is the part that matters.
We previously spent about US$155,000 a year on software subscriptions, before counting the work of keeping everything connected.  I have never been so damn happy to rethink that entire stack.

500,000 users is a milestone. Earning their trust and giving them a reason to stay is the job.

For every founder told they cannot compete without raising a fortune, I believe your odds are improving.  The next great software company may have fewer employees than its incumbent has recruiters.

Curious whether Automo could replace parts of your stack?  Check out the link in the comment.

Labor law doesn't stand still. Minimum wage updates, leave policy changes, new reporting requirements — they shift more often than most businesses have the bandwidth to track. And the discovery usually happens at the worst possible moment: mid-audit, or after an employee complaint has already been filed.

It's not negligence. It's that keeping every policy, contract, and process current with changing regulations, across every state or region a company operates in, is a full-time job in itself — one most HR teams are doing on the side of everything else.

AI compliance tools are starting to take that weight off. Platforms like Trakstar, ComplyAdvantage, and Zoho People now monitor regulatory changes automatically, flag outdated policies before they become liabilities, and keep an audit-ready paper trail on hiring, termination, and disciplinary decisions — the exact documentation that saves a company when a dispute does arise.

It doesn't replace legal judgment. It just means compliance gaps get caught in a quarterly review, not during an actual audit.

This is one of the areas we spend the most time on with clients at Raslery Consulting — because the cost of catching a gap early is nothing compared to the cost of missing it.

In June, SAG-AFTRA members ratified their new TV/Theatrical agreement with 91.42% approval. Among its provisions are stronger restrictions on synthetic performers and additional protections around digital replicas.

Producers wishing to use a synthetic in a human role must notify the union and bargain over its use, while the agreement establishes a principle favouring human performance. The WGA’s 2026 agreement moves into another part of the value chain: companies must now notify the Guild when writers’ work is licensed to train a commercial generative-AI system. 

These developments interest me because Hollywood is effectively asking a different AI-risk question. Much of the technology debate concentrates on the capabilities machines may acquire: autonomy, increasingly sophisticated reasoning and, at the extreme, whether future systems could become difficult for humans to control.

Creative workers are confronting the inverse question: as machines acquire more capabilities, what do humans retain control over?

Consider an actor’s face or voice. Historically, accessing the economic value of a performance generally required hiring the performer. Digital replication begins to separate the two. A person can perform once, while a technological representation of elements of that performance may potentially be reused elsewhere.

The economic asset is therefore no longer only labour. It can also become the reproducible digital representation of labour.

That changes the bargaining problem profoundly. Compensation is one issue, but so are consent, duration of use, ownership, reuse and the circumstances under which a synthetic alternative can substitute for another human engagement. SAG-AFTRA itself frames its AI guardrails around consent, compensation and control.
 
Writing introduces a related complication. Once existing creative work can contribute to systems capable of producing new outputs, the boundary between creation and productive input becomes harder to ignore. The WGA’s notification provision is significant precisely because it begins bringing the licensing of that input into the contractual relationship.
 
This is why I would not separate today’s labour disputes from the larger AI-risk conversation. They operate on different timescales, but they concern the same underlying allocation of power: what machines are permitted to do, what humans continue to control, and which institutions define the boundary between the two.

Long before we know whether humanity can retain control over the most advanced AI systems, contracts such as these are already determining something much more immediate:

- How much control humans retain over the economic value of their own identity and creative work.

Remote is a work arrangement. It is not automatically a hiring jurisdiction.

Across years in HR leadership and recruitment, I have seen how one word in a vacancy can create the wrong expectation.

A role is marked “remote,” so candidates understandably assume that location is no longer a barrier. But the employer may still be able to hire in only a limited number of countries.

Consider Epoch AI’s current Recruiter/Senior Recruiter vacancy⁠.

It is fully remote and says the organisation can employ people in many countries. It also explains that contracts and payments are usually localised.

That distinction matters.

The lesson is not that every remote job must be open worldwide. It is that flexibility and eligibility are different promises.

A clear remote vacancy should tell candidates:

Which countries or time zones are eligible?

Will they be employees or contractors?

In what currency will they be paid?

What travel or working-hour overlap is expected?

This information does more than improve candidate experience. It reduces unsuitable applications, protects the employer’s reputation and gives recruiters a more credible process to manage.

Before publishing your next remote vacancy, imagine that the strongest candidate lives in Abuja.

Can they tell from the advert whether you can legally employ and pay them?

If not, the job may be remote, but the opportunity is still unclear.
